chats.answer:
For editing 4K video directly from a NAS in Adobe Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, I'd prioritize 10GbE networking, sustained read speed, SSD caching or all-flash storage, and reliability over CPU power or NAS-specific video features.

My recommendation depends on whether you're editing compressed 4K H.264/H.265, ProRes, or multicam footage.

What matters most

Feature

	

Recommendation




Network

	

10GbE minimum for serious editing




Drive bays

	

6–8 bays for HDD, or 4+ SSD slots

RAID 6 HDD array or all-flash SSD




NAS CPU

	

Modern Intel/AMD; doesn't need to be extremely powerful




RAM

	

16–32GB




Protocol

	

SMB for Mac/Windows, or NFS where appropriate




Local workstation

	

Fast NVMe for media cache, previews and scratch files

A 10GbE connection provides about 900–1,100 MB/s in favorable real-world conditions, enough for many 4K workflows. But multiple high-bitrate streams, shared editors, and heavy scrubbing can make HDD latency a bigger issue than bandwidth.

How I'd connect it
For a single editor, a direct 10GbE Ethernet connection can avoid the cost of a 10GbE switch. Thunderbolt NAS networking is another option, but verify the exact model's support.

For Premiere, store source footage on the NAS but keep media cache and previews locally. For Resolve, keep cache, optimized media and the project library/database on a local SSD unless you're deliberately setting up a shared project server.

One important caveat: NVMe cache does not automatically make sustained editing faster. If you need consistently low latency, an actual SSD storage pool is more dependable.

For editing 4K video directly off a NAS in Adobe Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, I'd prioritize 10GbE networking, sustained disk performance, and SSD caching or all-flash storage over CPU power.

My top choices are QNAP for maximum performance, Synology for ease of use, and TrueNAS for a custom high-performance setup.

The biggest distinction is whether you're editing 4K H.264/H.265, ProRes, BRAW, or multiple multicam streams. A good NAS can handle all of these, but the hardware requirements differ significantly.

How I'd configure it

For an 8-bay NAS, I'd start with six to eight CMR NAS/enterprise hard drives, RAID 6 or RAIDZ2 for two-drive fault tolerance, 16–32GB RAM, and a dedicated 10GbE connection to the editing computer.

Keep Premiere's media cache, Resolve's render cache, and ideally active project databases on a local NVMe SSD. Store the original footage and shared media on the NAS. NVMe caching on the NAS is optional; it doesn't automatically make sustained video reads faster.

RAID protects against drive failures, but you still need a separate backup.

chats.answer:
For editing 4K video directly from a NAS in Adobe Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, I'd prioritize 10GbE networking, sustained disk performance, and reliability over CPU power or fancy NAS features.

My top choices are QNAP TVS-h874, Synology DS1825+, and QNAP TVS-h674.

The right choice depends on whether you're editing one or multiple 4K streams, using H.264/H.265 versus ProRes/DNxHR, and whether multiple editors need simultaneous access.

What performance do you actually need?

Workflow

	

Recommended sustained throughput




Single 4K H.264/H.265 stream

	

50–150 MB/s

100–200 MB/s




Multicam 4K editing

	

300–700 MB/s




Multiple editors / heavy 4K workflows

	

700–1,200+ MB/s

These are practical planning targets, not fixed requirements. Codec, frame rate, number of streams, and effects all matter.

A 10GbE connection tops out at approximately 1,250 MB/s theoretically, with real-world transfers commonly around 900–1,100 MB/s. That's why 10GbE is the sweet spot for serious 4K editing.

How I'd configure it

For a serious 4K editing setup:

NAS: 6–8 bays, preferably 8.

Drives: 6–8 CMR NAS/enterprise HDDs, RAID 6 or RAIDZ2.

Networking: Dedicated 10GbE between workstation and NAS.

RAM: 16–32GB or more for ZFS-based systems.

Cache: Keep Premiere media cache and Resolve render cache on your workstation's local NVMe SSD.

Protocol: SMB for straightforward cross-platform sharing.

Protection: Separate backup; RAID is not a backup.

For example, eight 12TB drives in RAID 6 provide approximately 72TB usable before filesystem overhead, with two-drive failure tolerance.

One important detail: SSD caching on the NAS doesn't automatically improve sequential video playback. For high-bitrate footage, more HDD spindles and faster networking can be more valuable.
